capability 1: task: copy a string after a separator prediction: With hand-set weights the probe at output step i matches the address written at input position i, so every string is copied exactly at every listed length when d grows with the log of the length.

capability 2: task: associative recall of K pairs prediction: With hand-set weights the first round binds each item to the one before it and the second retrieves the item stored after the matching one; per-query accuracy 1.0 at every listed K.

capability 3: task: two-type bracket nesting prediction: The legal closing bracket is predicted exactly up to depth D when the number of rounds grows with D; with two fixed rounds and fixed precision the error does not vanish for all depths as the length grows.

capability 4: task: two-hop lookup and chained assignments prediction: The first round retrieves g(x) and the second retrieves f at that point, so f(g(x)) is answered exactly; chained assignments need one round per link.

capability 5: task: parity of a long binary string prediction: With a fixed number of rounds and fixed precision, no setting of the weights decides the parity of every binary string as the length grows.

definitions.text: The model is the card's causal weighted-retrieval model. It retains separate address and content rows for each round and the current working vector h. Each round uses Wa, Wc, Wp, Wo, U and V, all square d-by-d matrices, with normalized exponential retrieval, residual additions and coordinatewise max(0,z), exactly as in the card. The ordinary model has two rounds. E and O are symbol embedding and readout matrices, and P supplies positional embedding rows. All these parameters are learned by gradient descent on next-symbol cross-entropy through both rounds in learnability statements; constructions instead hand-set them. No auxiliary parser, stack, key-value dictionary or external lookup is allowed.

For the cost reference, every matrix-vector product and the content-weighted sum use @. Scores are A @ p, divided by the Python-computed scalar sqrt(d); exponentials are evaluated without max subtraction; their sum uses np.sum, and normalization uses elementwise division. ReLU uses np.maximum. Predict computes h @ O and argmax at every token. Retained state consists only of A1,C1,A2,C2, current h and one Python integer t; temporary probes, weights, retrieved vectors and logits are not retained. Parameters are excluded from state. The position table is supplied as a fixed list of 4096 d-vector parameter rows before the cost run, independently of sequence length. Parameter keys are E, P, Wa, Wc, Wp, Wo, U, V, O; the six round-specific matrix keys contain lists of two matrices. E has shape (vocabulary,d), O has shape (d,vocabulary). Position indices start at zero.

Argmax ties choose the smallest token id. Construction and learning evaluation use the supplied task-contract generators and scoring positions, including self-fed copy continuation. Copy and dyck accuracy are per sequence; recall and composition accuracy are per query. Binding scores both requested constants. The mechanism executes its update on every supplied token, including separators and queries. P2 witnesses must implement D1 rather than replacing retrieval by direct indexing or a symbolic task solver.

Choose d=16*ceiling(log(2*L)/log(2)) for P2 copying and d=64 for the other P2 tasks. These are resource conventions where the card leaves the width unspecified, not claims that these widths suffice. Each construction uses two rounds, including nesting and binding; larger-depth and longer-chain checks are allowed to fail. Copy has 2*L positions and vocabulary 5. Recall has 3*K+1 positions, key universe 2*K, value universe 16 and vocabulary 2*K+17. Dyck supplies positional parameter rows for at most 4*depth tokens and vocabulary 4. Composition has 5*T+3 positions and vocabulary 3*T+3. Binding has 4*hops+7 positions, 2*hops+2 variables, 8 values and vocabulary 2*hops+11. Positional parameters are fixed for the task layout before any tokens arrive; token stores grow only as tokens arrive.

P4 uses d=64, two rounds and square feed-forward matrices. Selected cases are copy L=4, recall K=4, dyck depth=2 and composition T=4. Training and test instances use the supplied task generators; recall uses V=16 and n_keys=16. All matrices named in D1 are learned, with no hand-set task-rule member. Seeds are 0,1,2. Each seed uses the same prover-declared training recipe on true data, no data, and the same token sequences with randomized answers. The initialization distribution, gradient-descent implementation, learning rate, passes and batch size are chosen by the prover within the supplied P4 budget. Both controls and the replay requirement remain mandatory.

For analytical complexity, vocabulary size V is fixed independently of sequence length and model width. With the operation spelling of D2, define q(t,d,V)=12*d^2+4*t*d+8*t+7*d+d*V+V-3, Q(n,d,V)=2*d*n*(n+1)+4*n*(n+1)+n*(12*d^2+7*d+d*V+V-3), and S(n,d)=4*n*d+d+1. Theta means uniform positive lower and upper constant factors for all positive integer sequence lengths and widths, with constants permitted to depend on the fixed vocabulary. These analytical expressions describe execution of the equations, not an assertion that a fixed finite positional table supports arbitrarily long sequences.

The P5 sample account uses the card's declared restricted target-rule classes with uniform target selection and whole-instance examples. The task protocol supplies encodings and class restrictions, but no class member. Copy and recall classes are all functions from four indices or key ranks to four source indices or value ranks. The depth-two bracket class is all binary closer-label maps on the six listed nonempty stack contexts. The composition class is all selectors s on four arguments, answering f(g(s(x))). Prior bits are measured relative to these classes; parsing or lookup learnability is not inferred from this restricted-class account.

The P3 task family is next-symbol inference on binary token streams of arbitrary length using the fixed positional-table resource of the P1 reference. Solving an instance requires executing the specified embed, update and readout at every token; an undefined positional lookup is failure, regardless of the requested target symbols. P[t] is literal zero-based table indexing, with no wraparound, clipping, extrapolation, dynamic parameter creation or replacement position encoding. A table with N rows has valid indices Fin N. A valid lookup for each of M positions must preserve its zero-based integer index. P3 concerns this finite positional-resource limit only, not a parity or nesting lower bound.

not_formalized.why: P2.copy specifies the output construction, but the additional exact probe-address 'matches' assertion has no stated mathematical meaning or tolerance, so formalizing the whole conjunction would require inventing an internal invariant.
P2.recall checks the output task, but the additional first-round binding and second-round retrieval assertions specify neither an encoding nor an equality criterion for represented items.
The claim does not specify the round-growth function, width resources, finite-precision arithmetic semantics, or the distribution or worst-case quantifier underlying nonvanishing error.

P2.composition checks the output tasks, but exact intermediate retrieval and the necessity of one round per link are insufficiently specified to distinguish a representation invariant from a resource lower bound.

The asymptotic parity impossibility leaves width, positional parameter availability and finite-precision semantics unspecified, and the growing token store precludes substituting a fixed-state argument.

spec.equations:
def expected(params, sizes, tokens):
    d = sizes['d']
    addresses = [np.empty((0, d)), np.empty((0, d))]
    contents = [np.empty((0, d)), np.empty((0, d))]
    result = []
    for position, token in enumerate(tokens):
        h = np.asarray(params['E'][token]) + np.asarray(params['P'][position])
        for layer in range(2):
            a = np.asarray(params['Wa'][layer]) @ h
            c = np.asarray(params['Wc'][layer]) @ h
            p = np.asarray(params['Wp'][layer]) @ h
            addresses[layer] = np.concatenate((addresses[layer], a.reshape(1, d)), axis=0)
            contents[layer] = np.concatenate((contents[layer], c.reshape(1, d)), axis=0)
            scores = (addresses[layer] @ p) / (d ** 0.5)
            numerators = np.exp(scores)
            weights = numerators / np.sum(numerators)
            r = weights @ contents[layer]
            g = h + np.asarray(params['Wo'][layer]) @ r
            h = g + np.asarray(params['U'][layer]) @ np.maximum(0, np.asarray(params['V'][layer]) @ g)
        output = int(np.argmax(h @ np.asarray(params['O'])))
        state = {'A1': addresses[0].copy(), 'C1': contents[0].copy(), 'A2': addresses[1].copy(), 'C2': contents[1].copy(), 'h': h.copy(), 't': position + 1}
        result.append({'state': state, 'output': output})
    return result

hypothesis_class.definition: Sort the four distinct stored keys only to name ranks k_i and associated values v_i; all selectors s on the four ranks answer query k_i with v_s(i), with identity selector the target.

hypothesis_class.definition: All maps from the nonempty bottom-to-top contexts (0),(1),(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1) to the two closer tokens; the target returns the closer matching the top.
hypothesis_class.size_justification: Two choices for each of six contexts give 2^6=64; every context occurs in a valid depth-two prefix and distinguishes differing maps. The target map is not hand-set.

hypothesis_class.definition: All selectors s on four arguments, answering f(g(s(x))) for input tables f,g and request x; identity selector is the target.
hypothesis_class.size_justification: Four choices for each of four arguments give 4^4=256; tables that separate differing selected arguments distinguish any two selectors. No selector member is hand-set.
